q: How do I calculate emissions for an export container moved by truck, rail and ship?
title: Emissions for a truck, rail and ship container
short: Split the trip into legs, calculate each one as cargo weight x leg distance x that mode's factor, then add the legs and the terminal handling in between. ISO 14083 calls this a transport chain. Use the real route and the same factor basis, well-to-wheel, for every leg.
audience: Indian exporters shipping via ICDs, the Dedicated Freight Corridor and JNPA or Mundra

ol: Pre-carriage by road: factory to the ICD or rail siding.
Main carriage by rail: ICD to the port, often over the Dedicated Freight Corridor.
Sea leg: Indian port to the EU port, with any transhipment port.
On-carriage by road at destination, if you pay for it.
Hub operations: container handling at the ICD and at each port. ISO 14083 treats these as their own elements, with their own emissions.

ul: Road legs: the lorry receipt or e-way bill for distance; the packing list for weight.
Rail: the railway receipt or the container train operator's invoice, which names the ICD and port.

Sea: the bill of lading gives the port of loading, any transhipment and the port of discharge. Use the route actually sailed; a diversion round the Cape of Good Hope is far longer than the Suez route.
Your Incoterm decides which legs are yours. Under FOB you pay up to the ship; under CIF or DAP you also pay the sea leg and beyond.

sections.h: Choosing a factor for each leg
p: Use one basis for all legs: well-to-wheel CO2e per tonne-km, at average load with typical empty running included. For road legs, pick the truck class that carried the box; a loaded container usually moves on a tractor-trailer. The default for India rail covers diesel and electric traction together. A carrier's own factor can replace any default.
For sea, carriers often give factors per TEU-km. Convert with the cargo weight per TEU stated by the source, or stay per TEU throughout.

ul: Using one distance, port to port, for the whole chain.
Leaving out the road legs because they are short. Per tonne-km they are the most carbon intensive part.
Using the container's gross weight on one leg and cargo weight on another.
Adding an empty return trip or empty container repositioning on top of defaults that already include typical empty running.

example.title: Worked example: 20 t of cargo, Ludhiana to Rotterdam via Mundra
lines: Road, factory to ICD: 20 t x 25 km = 500 tonne-km x 0.0551 = 27.55 kg CO2e
Rail, ICD to Mundra: 20 t x 1,350 km = 27,000 tonne-km x 0.0106 = 286.2 kg CO2e
Sea, Mundra to Rotterdam via Suez: 20 t x 11,500 km = 230,000 tonne-km x 0.0084 = 1,932.0 kg CO2e
Road, Rotterdam to consignee: 20 t x 150 km = 3,000 tonne-km x 0.0551 = 165.3 kg CO2e
Transport legs total: 27.55 + 286.2 + 1,932.0 + 165.3 = 2,411.05 kg CO2e, about 2.41 t
Hub operations at the ICD, Mundra and Rotterdam: add from terminal or carrier data
example.note: Distances are illustrative. Factors are default intensities per tonne-km, well-to-wheel: tractor-trailer 0.0551, rail in India 0.0106, container ship 0.0084. Each already includes typical empty running, so no return trip is added. The Rotterdam road leg uses the Indian tractor-trailer default only to show the arithmetic; use the European carrier's factor for that leg.

senseible: Senseible reads weight and distance from freight bills where they are printed; a leg gets a figure only with both and an approved factor for its mode, otherwise it is marked as needing data. Its logistics calculator adds legs per tonne-km by mode and Indian truck class, uses a carrier's factor as given and adds no extra empty return uplift. Terminal handling figures come from your carrier or terminal.
